strengths: Significance: A training-only part-correspondence regularizer is a useful contribution to generalized category discovery. PartCo preserves the host method’s inference pipeline and reportedly improves several distinct baselines. Table 1 shows substantial DINOv2 SimGCD gains on CUB (+9.6 points), Stanford Cars (+7.4), and Aircraft (+12.6).

Empirical breadth: Evaluation covers fine-grained and generic datasets, multiple host methods, DINOv2/v3, and additional CLIP experiments. Supplementary experiments include long-tailed Herbarium19 and inaccurate category-count settings, extending the evidence beyond the primary benchmarks.

Soundness: Several ablations meaningfully investigate the proposed mechanism. The foreground-only control in Table I provides evidence that background suppression alone does not explain the gains; experiments also examine label granularity, unsupervised correspondence supervision, and alternative label construction.

Originality: Although part-aware GCD already exists, using frozen-feature correspondence assignments as auxiliary supervision without changing inference is a distinct, practically useful design. Section 5 explicitly distinguishes this approach from APL and PartGCD.

Presentation, limitations, and ethics: The overall pipeline is understandable, and runtime measurements and per-class failure analyses are useful. Section S5 appropriately acknowledges backbone and spatial-resolution limitations. No material research-ethics concern is apparent from the reported benchmark-based work.
weaknesses: Soundness—conflicting experimental results: Table 2 reports DINOv2 PartCo-SimGCD ImageNet-100 accuracy as 90.1/92.0/89.2 for All/Old/New, whereas Table G reports 94.6/96.7/92.0 for second-order labels with the identical baseline. Second-order labels are the recommended generic-dataset configuration, and Figure 7 supports the latter result. This unexplained discrepancy changes the claimed improvement from 0.2 to 4.7 points. Table 1 also reports CUB PartCo-SPTNet All accuracy of 82.6, exceeding both Old (82.3) and New (81.8), which is incompatible with a common matching and is not explained by independently optimal subset matching. These discrepancies require an audit of the evaluation and tables.

Soundness—the ablated objective does not match its definition: Equation 8 defines the auxiliary loss as (1−λb)L_unsup + λb L_sup, while λb also controls supervised/unsupervised baseline terms. Yet Section 4.3 describes λb as balancing PartCo against the baseline, and Table 4 treats λb=0 as recovering the original baseline. Under the stated equations, λb=0 retains the unsupervised part loss and changes the baseline objective. Consequently, the actual optimized objective and the interpretation of this ablation are unclear.

Reproducibility—central label construction is underspecified: Section 3.1 omits the candidate k range and selected cluster counts, PCA centering and sign conventions, and the score normalization needed to interpret a fixed objectness threshold of 0.6. It also leaves background handling, recursive second-order clustering, and alignment of offline labels with random training crops insufficiently specified. These choices directly determine the supervisory signal.

Reproducibility—loss implementation needs clarification: Equations 6–7 exclude positive sets from their denominators, unlike standard supervised contrastive loss, but do not explain this choice or fully specify the candidate feature indices. Feature normalization, treatment of absent parts and empty positive sets, and conversion of classifier probabilities into discrete pseudo-labels are not stated. An exact algorithm or implementation is needed to establish what was evaluated.

Evaluation reliability: Results lack seed counts and variability estimates despite randomness in the one-image-per-class PCA sample, clustering, and training. This particularly affects small gains such as +0.3 on Stanford Cars for PartCo-SelEx. The manuscript also does not explain a validation protocol for selecting projection dimension, loss balance, and label granularity without using discovery-set ground truth.

Significance and mechanistic evidence: The strongest configurations are competitive rather than uniformly superior: DINOv2 PartCo-SelEx averages 85.5 on SSB versus Hyp-SelEx’s 86.0, while PartCo-SimGCD reduces CIFAR100 novel accuracy from 87.2 to 83.0. Table F offers encouraging part-alignment evidence, but does not sufficiently specify the matching scope or explain the selection of eight grouped anatomical labels. Foreground-only controls do not isolate semantic correspondence from generic region-level regularization; shuffled correspondence or matched nonsemantic-region controls would strengthen that claim. Overall, the promising contribution is outweighed by unresolved reporting and reproducibility problems.

strengths: Significance: Training-only part supervision is a useful contribution to generalized category discovery. PartCo preserves the host method’s inference pipeline and reports substantial fine-grained improvements, including SimGCD’s average DINOv2 accuracy increasing from 69.0% to 78.8% across the three SSB datasets.

Originality: The distinctive contribution is using frozen-feature correspondence labels as auxiliary supervision across existing GCD methods. Section 5 reasonably distinguishes this approach from APL’s aggregated part representations and PartGCD’s learned decomposition.

Evaluation: Experiments cover several host methods, eight datasets, and DINOv2/v3 and CLIP backbones. The supplementary foreground-only control, estimated-category-count experiments, and compute measurements are useful additions.

Presentation and limitations: The overall pipeline is understandable and illustrated clearly. Sections S4–S5 acknowledge failure cases, patch-resolution constraints, and backbone dependencies. These candid limitations are appropriate; no material research-ethics concern is apparent.
weaknesses: Soundness: Important numerical inconsistencies undermine confidence in the evaluation. Table 1 reports CUB PartCo-SPTNet accuracy of 82.6% All, exceeding both Old (82.3%) and New (81.8%), which is incompatible with the stated partition-based metric. Table G reports 94.6% ImageNet-100 accuracy for second-order supervision on the SimGCD baseline, whereas Table 2 reports 90.1% for PartCo-SimGCD under the stated generic-dataset configuration. These discrepancies require corrected results and an explicit evaluation protocol.

Methodological consistency: Section 4.3 describes λb as balancing the baseline and proposed losses, and Table 4 treats λb=0 as the unmodified baseline. However, Equation 8 gives Lpc=(1−λb)Lunsup_pc+λbLsup_pc, so λb=0 retains unsupervised part supervision; λb also appears inside the baseline losses. The ablation therefore does not correspond to the stated objective, leaving the actual training procedure unclear.

Reproducibility: Core label-construction choices are missing, including the candidate range and selected values of k, PCA score normalization and sign handling for the fixed 0.6 foreground threshold, and the precise second-order clustering procedure. The manuscript also does not adequately specify how offline labels follow geometric augmentations or how absent parts and empty positive sets are handled.

Loss specification: Equations 6–7 exclude all positives from the denominator, unlike standard supervised contrastive learning, without explaining this choice. Feature normalization, anchor exclusion, and the conversion of probability vectors into discrete pseudo-labels are also unclear. These details materially affect the objective and should be specified and validated.

Evidence and significance: Results lack repeated-run uncertainty estimates, including sensitivity to the randomly selected image per known class used to fit the priors. This matters particularly for small improvements, such as the 0.3-point average generic-data gain for DINOv2 SimGCD. Claims of consistent improvement also need qualification: its CIFAR100 New accuracy decreases from 87.2% to 83.0%.

Mechanistic evidence: The foreground-only control is helpful but does not isolate correspondence quality from additional pooled-patch contrastive supervision. Matched controls using spatial partitions or shuffled correspondence assignments would strengthen the central explanation. Table F’s semantic-alignment results additionally need the cluster counts, matching scope, and rationale for evaluating only the selected CUB parts.

Overall assessment: The practical idea and reported gains merit further development, but unresolved inconsistencies in the results and training objective, together with missing implementation details, prevent the current manuscript from supporting reliable acceptance.

strengths: Significance: PartCo addresses a useful problem: exploiting local visual information for generalized category discovery without changing the host method’s inference pipeline. Table 1 reports substantial DINOv2 SimGCD gains on CUB (71.5→81.1), Stanford Cars (71.5→78.9), and Aircraft (63.9→76.5). Improvements across four host methods make the contribution broader than a single improved baseline.

Originality: Although part-based discovery and contrastive learning are established, using frozen-feature correspondence labels as training-only supervision is a useful distinction from methods that replace the image representation or introduce learned part decomposition. The discussion of APL and PartGCD appropriately identifies this distinction.

Empirical support: The evaluation covers eight datasets, DINOv2/v3 and CLIP backbones, and several complementary ablations. The foreground-only control in Table I is particularly helpful: its smaller gains support the value of additional part supervision beyond background removal. Experiments with estimated category counts also extend the standard known-count setting.

Presentation and practicality: The overall pipeline is understandable, with useful diagrams and extensive supplementary analysis. Table B reports modest training-time increases and unchanged inference, although memory rises from 8.6 to 12.0 GB.

Limitations and ethics: The manuscript openly discusses patch-resolution constraints, backbone requirements, and substantial per-class failures. These are useful qualifications rather than reasons for rejection. The benchmark-based study presents no evident material ethical concern.
weaknesses: Soundness: The objective and its ablation are inconsistent. Equation 8 defines the parametric part loss as (1−λb)Lunsup_pc + λbLsup_pc, so λb=0 retains unsupervised part supervision; nevertheless, Table 4 reports exactly the baseline results at zero and describes λb as balancing PartCo against the baseline. Earlier equations also use λb within the baseline losses. The actual weighting scheme must be specified before this central ablation can be interpreted.

Reproducibility: Equations 6–7 exclude all positives from the denominator, unlike standard supervised contrastive loss. This may be intentional, but the manuscript does not explain the choice or specify normalization of projected part features. Handling absent parts and empty positive sets is also unspecified, despite divisions by their cardinalities. These details materially affect the implemented objective.

Reproducibility: The central label-construction procedure lacks essential details: the candidate range and selected values of k, PCA score normalization and sign convention for the fixed 0.6 foreground threshold, treatment of masked background tokens, exact recursive clustering for second-order labels, and alignment of offline labels with random image augmentations. A complete algorithm and implementation settings are needed to reproduce the proposed supervision reliably.

Evidence consistency: Table G reports ImageNet-100 accuracy of 94.6/96.7/92.0 with second-order labels, starting from the SimGCD baseline of 89.9/95.5/87.1. Table 2 instead reports 90.1/92.0/89.2 for PartCo-SimGCD. No experimental difference explains this discrepancy. It changes the apparent improvement from 0.2 to 4.7 points and directly affects the claimed benefit of second-order labels.

Statistical support and scope: No repeated-run uncertainty is reported, despite random image selection for PCA, clustering, and training. This matters especially for small gains such as SelEx on Cars (82.2→82.5). Improvements are not uniform across old/new categories: DINOv2 SimGCD’s average generic-dataset New accuracy falls from 91.3 to 90.4. Claims of consistently improved discovery should distinguish overall accuracy from novel-category performance.

Mechanistic evidence: Foreground masking is a useful control, but it does not isolate semantic correspondence from the effects of an additional local contrastive objective. Matched spatial-grid or shuffled-correspondence controls would strengthen that attribution. Overall, the substantial empirical merits warrant serious consideration, but unresolved objective definitions, missing construction details, and inconsistent results prevent a confident acceptance recommendation.
